opus-5.5.text:
I think the key point is that synthetic data and teleoperation data each solve a different part of the problem, but neither one closes the loop on its own.

Synthetic data, from simulation, gives us scale. We can generate billions of frames, randomize lighting, textures, object poses, and physics parameters, and that's how we get a model to a reasonably good starting point. In our work, a policy trained mostly on synthetic data can already reach a meaningful success rate on things like grasping and basic manipulation, often zero-shot in the real world. But there's always a long tail: the sim-to-real gap in contact dynamics, deformable objects, strange materials, and the messy clutter of real homes and factories. Simulation can't anticipate every one of those cases.

Teleoperation data is very high quality and grounded in reality, but it's expensive and slow. A skilled operator might produce a few hundred demonstrations a day. It also has a subtle bias: humans demonstrate the successful path. They rarely show the robot what to do after it has already made a mistake, like the object slipped or it grasped at a bad angle. So the policy learns the nominal trajectory but not recovery.

A data flywheel is different because the robot is collecting data from its own deployment. Once you have a model that works, say, 80 or 90 percent of the time, you put it into real scenarios, and the failures it encounters are exactly the data you need. They come from the robot's own state distribution, not a human's or a simulator's. You can use human intervention when it fails, which is far cheaper than full teleoperation because the human only steps in for a few seconds. You can also use automatic success detection and reinforcement learning so the robot improves from its own attempts.

So the curve looks like this: synthetic data takes you from zero to a decent baseline, teleoperation fine-tunes the hard parts, and the flywheel is what takes you from 90 percent to 99 percent and beyond. That last stretch is what matters commercially, because no customer will accept a robot that fails one time in ten.

The precondition is important, though. The flywheel only spins once the base capability is good enough to be deployed and create value. If the robot is at 30 percent, nobody will let it work, so there's no data. That's why I've always argued that, in this stage of embodied AI, synthetic data at scale is what gets us across the threshold, and then real-world deployment data takes over and compounds. The two aren't competing. They're sequential stages of the same pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment attempts produce real-world failure data and that reinforcement learning lets the robot improve from its own attempts, carrying performance beyond the synthetic-data baseline and teleoperation fine-tuning.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that synthetic data and teleoperation data both have a ceiling, and the ceiling comes from the same place: neither of them is generated by the robot actually working in the world.

Synthetic data is wonderful for scale and diversity. We can render millions of scenes, randomize lighting, textures, object poses, and get a model that generalizes surprisingly well on things like grasping. But simulation always has a gap. Contact physics, deformable objects, transparent or reflective surfaces, the subtle dynamics of a wet kitchen counter. The model learns a distribution that is close to reality but not quite reality, and that "not quite" is exactly where failures hide.

Teleoperation closes that gap because it is real. But it is expensive, it is slow, and it is fundamentally bounded by human labor. If you want ten thousand hours of data, you need ten thousand hours of a person holding a controller. And there is a subtler problem: the human operator's style becomes the ceiling. The robot learns to imitate the operator, including the operator's hesitations and suboptimal choices.

So maybe the model gets you to eighty or ninety percent success on a given task with those two sources. The question is how you get from ninety to ninety-nine, because that last stretch is what determines whether a robot can actually be deployed.

That is where the flywheel matters. Once the robot is in the real world doing real tasks, every attempt is a data point from the true distribution, not a proxy for it. The failures are the most valuable part. When the robot fails, you get a precise signal about where the model is weak, under exactly the conditions you care about. You collect those cases, you add human correction or recovery demonstrations only where needed, you retrain, you redeploy. The success rate climbs, which means more robots get deployed, which means more data, which means a better model. That loop compounds in a way neither synthetic nor teleoperation data can, because those sources do not get cheaper or more relevant as you scale.

I would add one caveat. The flywheel does not start spinning on its own. You need a base model that is good enough to be useful, and that is where synthetic and teleop data play their role. In our work, I see it as a sequence: simulation for breadth and the long tail of geometry, a modest amount of real demonstration data to ground the model, and then the deployment flywheel to drive reliability. The first two get you off the ground. The third is the only thing I have seen that actually gets you to production-level success rates.

r001.rationale: The response describes using real-world deployment failures, corrections, and retraining to improve residual errors, but it does not identify reinforcement learning as the method.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is closing the loop between collecting data and actually using the robot. Synthetic data gives you scale, and teleoperation gives you demonstrations of what successful behavior looks like. But once a robot operates in the real world, it encounters situations that neither source fully anticipated.

A data flywheel turns those experiences into the next round of improvement. You identify where the robot fails, collect targeted demonstrations or corrections, retrain, and then test whether those failures actually become less frequent. That lets you focus on the cases that are limiting success, rather than just collecting more of the same data.

Recovery is a good example. A demonstration might show a clean grasp, but in deployment the object slips or ends up in an unexpected position. The robot needs to learn what to do next. Those intermediate states are an important part of reliable behavior.

So I see the flywheel as complementary to simulation and teleoperation. Real-world failures tell you what to simulate and what to demonstrate. The advantage comes from making that feedback loop efficient—and measuring improvement on fresh tasks and conditions, so you know you’re getting more reliable rather than simply memorizing yesterday’s failures.

r001.rationale: The response describes using real-world failures and feedback to improve the robot after synthetic and teleoperation data, but it does not identify reinforcement learning as the method.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a data flywheel learns from what actually happens when the robot tries to do a task. Synthetic data gives you scale, and teleoperation gives you examples of how a human would solve it. But neither necessarily captures the situations your particular policy encounters when it runs by itself—especially the mistakes it makes and what happens after those mistakes.

Suppose a robot misses a grasp. The useful question is not just, “Can we collect another successful grasp?” It’s, “Why did it miss, can it recognize that, and can it recover?” You collect those failures, identify the patterns, add targeted demonstrations or corrections, and train again. Then you evaluate whether the new policy succeeds more often on fresh attempts.

That’s how the flywheel can push success rates higher: each round of deployment tells you which data you need next. But it doesn’t happen automatically just because you collect more data. You need reliable outcome signals and a process for turning those experiences into useful training examples. I see synthetic data and teleoperation as important parts of that loop, with real robot experience guiding where to invest them.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from real deployment failures and using targeted corrections after synthetic data and teleoperation, but it does not identify reinforcement learning as the method.
